body.heading: The unbeatable strategy nobody can play
paragraphs: Against a perfectly random opponent, rock paper scissors has no winning strategy - every throw wins, loses and draws a third of the time. The catch is that humans cannot throw randomly. We have favourites, rhythms and superstitions, and every habit is a leak that an observant opponent can exploit.

The leaks are remarkably consistent. Beginners throw rock most often - it feels strong - and scissors least. Studies of casual players also find that men, on average, open with rock more than women do. Simply playing paper against a brand-new opponent already gives you a small statistical head start, before any psychology begins.

body.heading: Winners repeat, losers switch
paragraphs: In 2014, researchers at Zhejiang University ran a large tournament study - hundreds of students playing thousands of rounds - and found a clear rhythm: players who win a round tend to repeat their winning throw, while players who lose tend to switch, often to the throw that would have beaten the one that just beat them.

That rhythm suggests a counter-strategy. If you just lost, your opponent will probably repeat - so play the throw that beats their last one. If you just won, your opponent will probably switch to the throw that beats yours - so switch first, to the throw that beats that one. You are no longer playing the hands; you are playing the pattern of the person.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: With a friend's cheerful consent, tally their throws over 30 rounds without saying why. Then look for habits: favourite throws, favourite openings, and what they do immediately after losing. Most people are startled by how predictable their own column of tallies looks.

Then flip the exercise: try to throw genuinely randomly for 30 rounds, perhaps by secretly using the second hand of a clock to choose. Feeling how unnatural true randomness is explains every leak you found in your friend.

takeaway: Against a truly random player nobody has an edge - but people repeat after wins and switch after losses, and that rhythm can be read.
